front: Bonjour madame, je voudrais une baguette pas trop cuite.
pronunciation: [bohn-ZHOOR mah-DAM, zhuh voo-dreh zün bah-GET pah troh KWEET]
back: Hello madam, I'd like a baguette that's not too well done.
context: Always say 'bonjour' before anything else in a shop. Skipping it is considered rude.

front: On se fait combien de bises ici ?
pronunciation: [ohn suh feh kohm-byan duh BEEZ ee-SEE]
back: How many kisses do people give here?
context: Two in Paris, three around Montpellier, sometimes four in parts of the north. Even the French ask.

front: Une tradition alsacienne ? Je ne connaissais pas.
pronunciation: [ün trah-dee-SYOHN al-zah-SYEN ? zhuh nuh koh-neh-seh PAH]
back: An Alsatian tradition? I didn't know about it.
context: Regions are a source of pride. Showing curiosity about local customs is always appreciated.

front: Merci pour l'invitation, j'apporte quelque chose ?
pronunciation: [mehr-SEE poor lan-vee-tah-SYOHN, zhah-port kel-kuh SHOHZ]
back: Thanks for the invitation, shall I bring something?
context: Bring flowers, chocolates or wine. Don't be offended if your wine isn't opened: the host has planned the meal.

front: Ne coupe pas le nez du fromage !
pronunciation: [nuh koop pah luh nay dü froh-MAHZH]
back: Don't cut the tip off the cheese!
context: Cut wedges lengthwise so everyone gets some of the rind and some of the heart.

front: On ne coupe pas la salade, on la plie.
pronunciation: [ohn nuh koop pah lah sah-LAD, ohn lah PLEE]
back: You don't cut the salad, you fold it.
context: Old table etiquette: fold lettuce leaves with your fork and knife.

front: Ne pose pas le pain à l'envers, ça porte malheur.
pronunciation: [nuh pohz pah luh pan ah lahn-VEHR, sah port mah-LUHR]
back: Don't put the bread upside down, it's bad luck.
context: An old superstition, still respected in many families.

front: On commence par l'apéro, puis on passe à table.
pronunciation: [ohn koh-mahns par lah-pay-ROH, pwee ohn pas ah TAH-bluh]
back: We start with drinks and nibbles, then sit down to eat.
context: A dinner can last four hours: apéro, entrée, plat, fromage, dessert, café.

front: Je n'en peux plus, c'était délicieux.
pronunciation: [zhuh nahn puh PLÜ, say-teh day-lee-SYUH]
back: I can't eat another bite, it was delicious.
context: The polite way to refuse a second helping.

front: Combien tu gagnes ? – Ça, on ne le demande pas.
pronunciation: [kohm-byan tü GAN-yuh ? – SAH, ohn nuh luh duh-mahnd PAH]
back: How much do you earn? – That's something you don't ask.
context: Money is a taboo topic in France, even among friends.

front: Tu votes pour qui ?
pronunciation: [tü vot poor KEE]
back: Who do you vote for?
context: A question many French people consider private: 'le secret de l'isoloir'.

front: Encore une grève ? Ça ne m'étonne pas.
pronunciation: [ahn-kor ün GREV ? sah nuh may-tun PAH]
back: Another strike? I'm not surprised.
context: Strikes are part of French life, and so is complaining about them.

front: Râler, c'est un sport national.
pronunciation: [rah-LAY, seh tan spor nah-syoh-NAL]
back: Grumbling is a national sport.
context: 'Râler' = to moan. Complaining is often a way to bond.

front: C'était la croix et la bannière pour trouver une place.
pronunciation: [say-teh lah krwah ay lah bah-NYEHR poor troo-vay ün PLAS]
back: It was a real ordeal to find a parking space.
context: 'La croix et la bannière' (the cross and the banner) = a huge hassle.

front: On a cherché toute la journée, mais on a fait chou blanc.
pronunciation: [ohn nah shehr-SHAY toot lah zhoor-NAY, meh ohn nah feh shoo BLAHN]
back: We searched all day but came up empty-handed.
context: 'Faire chou blanc' = to fail, draw a blank.

front: Elle s'est mise sur son trente et un pour le mariage.
pronunciation: [el seh meez sür sohn trahnt ay AN poor luh mah-RYAHZH]
back: She got dressed to the nines for the wedding.
context: 'Se mettre sur son trente et un' = to dress up.

front: Il y a anguille sous roche.
pronunciation: [eel yah ahn-GEE soo ROSH]
back: There's something fishy going on.
context: Literally 'there's an eel under the rock'.

front: Depuis qu'il a perdu son emploi, il tire le diable par la queue.
pronunciation: [duh-pwee keel ah pehr-dü soh nahm-PLWAH, eel teer luh DYAH-bluh par lah KUH]
back: Since he lost his job, he's been struggling to make ends meet.
context: 'Tirer le diable par la queue' (pull the devil by the tail) = to be broke.

front: Il a eu son permis les doigts dans le nez.
pronunciation: [ee lah ü sohn pehr-MEE lay dwah dahn luh NAY]
back: He passed his driving test with no effort at all.
context: 'Les doigts dans le nez' (fingers up the nose) = easily.

front: Vers seize heures, j'ai toujours un coup de barre.
pronunciation: [vehr sez UHR, zhay too-zhoor an koo duh BAR]
back: Around 4 p.m., I always hit a wall.
context: 'Un coup de barre' = sudden tiredness.

front: Ne me raconte pas de bobards.
pronunciation: [nuh muh rah-kohnt pah duh boh-BAR]
back: Don't tell me fibs.
context: 'Un bobard' = a lie (informal).

front: J'ai le seum, on a perdu le match.
pronunciation: [zhay luh SUM, ohn nah pehr-dü luh MATCH]
back: I'm gutted, we lost the match.
context: Youth slang from Arabic: 'avoir le seum' = to be bitter, frustrated.

front: Ça me fait une belle jambe !
pronunciation: [sah muh feh tün bel ZHAHMB]
back: A fat lot of good that does me!
context: Ironic: that's no use to me at all.

front: Il avait un verre dans le nez.
pronunciation: [ee lah-veh tan VEHR dahn luh NAY]
back: He'd had one too many.
context: A humorous euphemism for being tipsy.

front: Je suis chocolat, le magasin est fermé.
pronunciation: [zhuh swee shoh-koh-LAH, luh mah-gah-zan eh fehr-MAY]
back: I'm out of luck, the shop is closed.
context: 'Être chocolat' = to be done for, disappointed.

front: C'est dimanche, tout est fermé sauf la boulangerie.
pronunciation: [seh dee-MAHNSH, too teh fehr-MAY sohf lah boo-lahnzh-REE]
back: It's Sunday, everything's closed except the bakery.
context: Many shops close on Sundays; some also close on Monday mornings.

front: Ici, on ne dérange pas les gens entre midi et deux.
pronunciation: [ee-SEE, ohn nuh day-rahnzh pah lay ZHAHN ahn-truh mee-DEE ay DUH]
back: Here, you don't disturb people between noon and two.
context: Lunchtime is sacred, especially in the provinces.

front: Au restaurant, on ne parle pas trop fort.
pronunciation: [oh res-toh-RAHN, ohn nuh parl pah troh FOR]
back: In restaurants, people don't talk too loudly.
context: Speaking loudly marks you as a tourist.

front: L'addition, c'est à vous de la demander.
pronunciation: [lah-dee-SYOHN, seh tah VOO duh lah duh-mahn-DAY]
back: It's up to you to ask for the bill.
context: Bringing it unasked would seem like rushing you out.

front: Le service est compris, le pourboire est un geste.
pronunciation: [luh sehr-vees eh kohm-PREE, luh poor-bwahr eh tan ZHEST]
back: Service is included; a tip is a gesture.
context: Leaving a few coins is appreciated, but 15–20% isn't expected.

front: On peut avoir une carafe d'eau, s'il vous plaît ?
pronunciation: [ohn puh tah-vwahr ün kah-raf DOH, seel voo PLEH]
back: Could we have a jug of tap water, please?
context: Restaurants must serve tap water free of charge.

front: Au café, c'est moins cher au comptoir qu'en terrasse.
pronunciation: [oh kah-FAY, seh mwan SHEHR oh kohn-TWAHR kahn teh-RAS]
back: In a café, it's cheaper at the counter than on the terrace.
context: Many cafés have different prices depending on where you drink.

front: Un petit noir, s'il vous plaît.
pronunciation: [an puh-tee NWAHR, seel voo PLEH]
back: An espresso, please.
context: 'Un petit noir' / 'un express' = an espresso. Ordering a cappuccino after lunch raises eyebrows.

front: Le samedi soir, on refait le monde autour d'une bouteille.
pronunciation: [luh sahm-dee SWAHR, ohn ruh-feh luh MOHND oh-toor dün boo-TAY]
back: On Saturday nights, we put the world to rights over a bottle.
context: 'Refaire le monde' = to have long political or philosophical discussions.

front: Il faut toujours vouvoyer les beaux-parents au début.
pronunciation: [eel foh too-zhoor voo-vwah-yay lay boh-pah-RAHN oh day-BÜ]
back: You should always use 'vous' with your in-laws at first.
context: Wait for them to suggest 'tu'. Some families keep 'vous' for life.

front: Il vaut mieux attendre qu'on vous propose de se tutoyer.
pronunciation: [eel voh myuh ah-tahn-druh kohn voo proh-pohz duh suh tü-twah-YAY]
back: It's better to wait until you're offered 'tu'.
context: At work, colleagues often use 'tu' quickly, but not always with the boss.

front: Avant d'envoyer un mail formel, vérifiez la formule de politesse.
pronunciation: [ah-vahn dahn-vwah-yay an mel for-MEL, vay-ree-fyay lah for-mül duh poh-lee-TES]
back: Before sending a formal email, check the closing formula.
context: 'Bien cordialement' is the safe default at work.

front: On est en août : Paris est vide.
pronunciation: [ohn neh tahn NOOT : pah-REE eh VEED]
back: It's August: Paris is empty.
context: Many businesses close for 'les grandes vacances'.

front: Cette année, le 8 mai tombe un jeudi : on fait le pont.
pronunciation: [set ah-NAY, luh wee MEH tohmb an zhuh-DEE : ohn feh luh POHN]
back: This year May 8 is a Thursday, so we're taking Friday off.
context: May is full of public holidays: 1 May, 8 May, Ascension and sometimes Whit Monday.

front: Les soldes commencent mercredi.
pronunciation: [lay SOLD koh-mahns mehr-kruh-DEE]
back: The sales start on Wednesday.
context: Sale dates are fixed by law: in January and in summer.

front: Il faut prendre un ticket et attendre son tour.
pronunciation: [eel foh prahn-druh an tee-KEH ay ah-tahn-druh sohn TOOR]
back: You have to take a ticket and wait your turn.
context: Jumping the queue ('griller la file') is badly received.

front: Je ne mange jamais de pain avec les pâtes.
pronunciation: [zhuh nuh mahnzh zhah-meh duh PAN ah-vek lay PAHT]
back: I never eat bread with pasta.
context: Bread is eaten with almost everything else, placed directly on the tablecloth.

front: On ne met pas de ketchup sur le steak tartare.
pronunciation: [ohn nuh meh pah duh ket-SHUP sür luh stek tar-TAR]
back: You don't put ketchup on steak tartare.
context: French cooks can be very firm about how a dish should be eaten.

front: Le pastis se boit avec de l'eau fraîche.
pronunciation: [luh pas-TEES suh bwah ah-vek duh loh FRESH]
back: Pastis is drunk with cold water.
context: The aniseed aperitif of the south, about five parts water to one.

front: S'il te taquine, c'est qu'il t'aime bien.
pronunciation: [seel tuh tah-KEEN, seh keel tem BYAN]
back: If he teases you, it means he likes you.
context: Teasing is a form of affection. Being able to tease back is a sign of integration.

front: Tu es devenu plus français que les Français !
pronunciation: [tü eh duh-vuh-nü plü frahn-SEH kuh lay frahn-SEH]
back: You've become more French than the French!
context: The ultimate compliment for a newcomer.

front: Je rêve en français maintenant.
pronunciation: [zhuh rev ahn frahn-SEH mant-NAHN]
back: I dream in French now.
context: Many learners notice this as a milestone of fluency.

front: Je ne comprends pas toutes les blagues, mais je ris quand même.
pronunciation: [zhuh nuh kohm-prahn pah toot lay BLAG, meh zhuh ree kahn MEM]
back: I don't get all the jokes, but I laugh anyway.
context: Humor is the last frontier of a foreign language.

front: Vous avez un léger accent, vous êtes d'où ?
pronunciation: [voo zah-vay an lay-zhay ak-SAHN, voo zet DOO]
back: You have a slight accent, where are you from?
context: Usually a sign of interest, not criticism.

front: Félicitations, vous parlez français comme un natif !
pronunciation: [fay-lee-see-tah-SYOHN, voo par-lay frahn-SEH kum an nah-TEEF]
back: Congratulations, you speak French like a native!
context: You've completed the course. Bravo!
